comments.author: Alexander Terp
comments.body:
Done for everything short of the seam. The core, the herdr adapter, the VT bindings, the bridge, the grid oracle and the perf harness are Rust; all 73 conformance cases run in both languages and the gate reports the count on every run.

Two proofs that mattered more than the green suite. The key-encoder survey snapshots and both grid snapshots pass unregenerated, so the Rust code drives libghostty to byte-identical output. And './dev --contract' runs the real app against a real daemon with the Rust bridge - which needed no FFI, because a separate process needs no seam.

Perf moved with the code it measures: frame.decode 5.96 -> 0.80 ns/byte, input.encode 162 -> 40 ns/key, frame.vt_parse flat at 3.72 -> 3.91 (the same libghostty call in both, so its flatness is what says the other two are real).

What stays Swift until the seam lands (a_27HFQbwG6): the window, the renderer, PaneInput's callers, and the key encoder the app still calls directly.

creator: Alexander Terp
description:
MIP-1. Move keymap, input pipeline, composition arbiter, frame decoding, diagnostics and the herdr adapter to Rust, with the conformance corpus as the acceptance criterion rather than a reading of the Swift tests.

Sequenced deliberately: port what already works and is covered before writing anything new on top, so a wrong seam surfaces on code we trust. herdr's src/ghostty/mod.rs is a working reference for driving libghostty-vt's key encoder from Rust, which is the fiddliest part.

Blocked on the corpus extraction (a_27HFEWM52) landing first.
title: Port the core to Rust, against the corpus
